templates.pattern: A field has an area of [A] m² and contains [N] individuals of a species. Calculate the population density in individuals per m².
templates.explanation:
Population density = number of individuals ÷ area
= [N] ÷ [A]
= [RESULT] individuals/m²

Population density allows comparison between populations in different sized areas. High density populations may face greater competition for resources and higher disease transmission rates.

templates.pattern: In a mark-recapture study [M] animals are caught and marked. In a second sample of [n] animals [m] are found to be marked. Calculate the estimated population size using the Lincoln-Petersen method.
templates.explanation:
Population estimate N = M × n ÷ m
= [M] × [n] ÷ [m]
= [RESULT]

This assumes the marked animals mix randomly with the unmarked population. Assumptions: no births, deaths or migration between samples and marking does not affect survival.

templates.pattern: A population of [P] individuals has [B] births in one year. Calculate the birth rate per 1000 individuals.
templates.explanation:
Birth rate = (births ÷ population) × 1000
= ([B] ÷ [P]) × 1000
= [RESULT] per 1000

Birth rates are expressed per 1000 to allow fair comparison between populations of different sizes. High birth rates are typical in developing countries with limited access to contraception.

templates.pattern: A population of [P] individuals has [D] deaths in one year. Calculate the death rate per 1000 individuals.
templates.explanation:
Death rate = (deaths ÷ population) × 1000
= ([D] ÷ [P]) × 1000
= [RESULT] per 1000

Death rates decrease with improved healthcare and nutrition. The difference between birth rate and death rate gives the natural increase rate of a population.

templates.pattern: A population has a birth rate of [B] per 1000 and a death rate of [D] per 1000. Calculate the natural increase rate per 1000.
templates.explanation:
Natural increase rate = birth rate − death rate
= [B] − [D]
= [RESULT] per 1000

A positive natural increase means the population is growing. A negative value means the population is declining. Many European countries have negative natural increase rates.

templates.pattern: A trophic level contains [E] kJ of energy. Calculate the energy available to the next trophic level assuming 10% efficiency.
templates.explanation:
Energy at next level = current energy × 10%
= [E] × 10 ÷ 100
= [RESULT] kJ

Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. The rest is lost as heat through respiration, egestion and decomposition. This limits food chains to 4-5 levels.

templates.pattern: A trophic level has [E] kJ of energy and an energy-to-biomass conversion factor of [C] kJ/g. Calculate the biomass of this trophic level in grams.
templates.explanation:
Biomass = energy ÷ conversion factor
= [E] ÷ [C]
= [RESULT] g

Different organisms have different energy-to-biomass ratios depending on their chemical composition. Fat has more energy per gram than carbohydrate or protein.

templates.pattern: A population of [N] individuals has [B] births and [D] deaths per year. Calculate the population growth rate as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Population growth rate = (births − deaths) ÷ population × 100
= ([B] − [D]) ÷ [N] × 100
= [B-D] ÷ [N] × 100
= [RESULT]%

Growth rate combines birth and death rates relative to population size. It does not include migration. A 2% growth rate doubles a population in about 35 years.

templates.pattern: An ecosystem has [PREY] prey animals and [PRED] predator animals. Calculate the prey to predator ratio.
templates.explanation:
Prey to predator ratio = prey population ÷ predator population
= [PREY] ÷ [PRED]
= [RESULT]

A healthy ecosystem typically has many more prey than predators. The ratio varies by ecosystem — African savannas have about 50-100 prey per predator. Disrupting this ratio destabilises the food web.

templates.pattern: A quadrat survey records [S1] species A, [S2] species B, [S3] species C and [S4] species D. Calculate the total species richness.
templates.explanation:
Total species richness = sum of all species counts
= [S1] + [S2] + [S3] + [S4]
= [RESULT]

Species richness is the simplest measure of biodiversity — just counting the number of different species present. It does not account for the relative abundance of each species.
